children: Arindam Majumder New Delhi: An Air India pilot was removed from an aircraft before take-off at Zurich airport after he was found to be under the influence of alcohol, intensifying scrutiny over the airline's safety culture amid a series of cases involving its crew. The incident, on September 6, forced rescheduling of the Delhi-bound flight and prompted the Swiss aviation regulator to alert its Indian counterpart.

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has since asked Air India to strengthen safeguards, people familiar with the matter said. "The responsibility for the further handling of this case lies with the DGCA as the competent authority of the state of the operator," a spokesperson of the Swiss Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA) told ET. The latest incident where an Air India crew broke rules has increased the challenge for incoming Air India CEO Tewolde Gebremariam who has set building a safety culture as his priority.

Early this month, the airline sacked a pilot who had tested positive for psychoactive substances after a Phuket-Delhi flight that he commanded momentarily lost altitude, injuring 24 passengers, in August. In another incident in January, an Air India pilot was detained at Vancouver airport after he reportedly smelled of alcohol shortly before boarding an aircraft.

An Air India spokesperson said the airline maintains a zero-tolerance policy towards any violation of safety, regulatory protocols. "Any confirmed breach is dealt with firmly and action in accordance with regulatory requirements and company policy is enforced," he said. Senior Air India executives said the incident in Zurich was reported by its own staff, which showed that its safety monitoring system is effective. "There will be some bad apples. The expectation is that responsible colleagues will report on any dereliction in duty," one of them said. "Safety remains the cornerstone of Air India. The objective is to ensure that every employee, particularly those in safety-critical roles, understands and upholds their responsibility." People aware of the incident said staffers of ground handling agencies found that the pilot was smelling of alcohol and alerted the authorities.

FOCA said it has taken action against the pilot under the regulations after a sobriety test indicated blood alcohol content of more than permissible limit. India's leading airlines Air India and IndiGo both have a zero-tolerance policy where even a minor trace of alcohol is considered as violation.

Pilots have to undergo a mandatory drug test before flights originating from India, but while arriving from many foreign airports, the test happens after landing. Senior pilots blamed growing disconnect between senior management and pilots as the reason for such lapses in safety culture. "There is a yawning gap between the top management and the flying pilots," a senior Air India captain said on condition of anonymity. "The top management is chasing growth.

The people flying the aircraft are not getting the attention they deserve." Air India executives cited above, however, said the airline has increased leadership engagement with flight crew to reinforce safety and professional standards and is providing multiple support mechanisms for crew members and employees. "Fleet-specific engagement sessions have also been expanded to include discussions on health, wellbeing, decision-making and professional responsibilities, with participation from relevant domain experts," one of them said.

title: Zurich Incident Adds to AI's Growing Crew Woes
